planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in late summer or early fall, choosing a site in full sun to part sun; leave the planting undisturbed for years so it can bulk up into a dense colony.

directions: This is the carmine-to-magenta-pink-flowered botanical variety of the familiar red oxblood lily, sold in the trade as the Pink or Carmine Oxblood Lily. Leafless flower stems push up in late summer to early fall, each topped by a cluster of small, mini-hippeastrum-like trumpets that open well before the strap-shaped foliage appears; the leaves then persist through winter and go dormant by late spring. Give it the same lean, dry, well-drained conditions as the species — rich soil and excessive water or fertilizer reduce flowering and can cause bulb rot. Once established, avoid digging or dividing it; clumps are long-lived and slowly multiply into dense, reliably naturalizing colonies.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep and 12-16 inches apart after the last frost in well-drained, sandy, alkaline soil in full sun; where winters are colder than zone 8, lift and store bulbs dry over winter.

directions: Also sold as Harrison's Orientred, this selected clone of the Aztec lily is far more vigorous and floriferous than the ordinary species, capable of pushing out several successive flushes of its brilliant velvety-red, orchid-like blooms across a single growing season rather than just one spring flush. Grow it exactly as you would the species: plant in gritty, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun, keep the bulbs on the dry side while dormant, and let the strap-shaped foliage mature fully before trimming it back. Because it blooms so repeatedly, it rewards slightly richer feeding than the straight species during active growth. Where winters are too cold for it to stay in the ground, lift the bulbs before frost and store them dry and cool until the following spring.
